title: Count the number of distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m by n grid, moving only right or down. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the single-row optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Unique Paths (Count Grid Routes Moving Only Right or Down)

s1_definition.profdef: Unique Paths counts routes from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid when only rightward and downward moves are allowed. The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above it and the cell to its left, with the top row and left column each having exactly one path. The grid reduces to a single row updated left to right.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India models an approval workflow drawn as a grid, where a request can only move to the next stage or to the next department, and it counts how many distinct approval routes exist from start to final sign-off.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ways to a cell equal ways from above plus ways from the left.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unique Paths counts routes from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid when only rightward and downward moves are allowed. The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above it and the cell to its left, with the top row and left column each having exactly one path. The grid reduces to a single row updated left to right.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India models an approval workflow drawn as a grid, where a request can only move to the next stage or to the next department, and it counts how many distinct approval routes exist from start to final sign-off.

**One line to remember:** Ways to a cell equal ways from above plus ways from the left.

sections.s2_technical:
Every cell can only be entered from directly above or directly to the left, and those two groups of paths are completely distinct, so the count at a cell is the sum of the counts of those two neighbours. The entire top row has exactly one path, moving only right, and the entire left column has exactly one path, moving only down, which gives the base cases. We fill the grid and read the bottom-right cell.

Because each row depends only on the row above and the cell to the left, a single row suffices: `int[] dp = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(dp, 1); for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) dp[j] += dp[j - 1]; return dp[n - 1];`, where `dp[j]` before the addition is the cell above and `dp[j - 1]` is the cell to the left. A concrete check: a three by seven grid has twenty-eight unique paths. Senior nuance: the time is the product of the dimensions and the space is the smaller dimension; there is also a closed-form binomial answer choosing the down moves among the total moves, which is constant time but risks overflow.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models a loan approval workflow as a grid, where a request advances either to the next approval stage or across to the next department, and risk analysts want to count the number of distinct approval routes from intake to final sign-off, to understand process complexity. Enumerating all routes by hand explodes combinatorially. This is exactly how Unique Paths works: the routes to a point are the sum of the routes from above and from the left.

The code defines a `WorkflowPathService` with `countApprovalRoutes(stages, departments)` using the single-row dynamic programming. A `Demo` sets a grid size and logs the number of routes.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a workflow grid of three stages by seven departments. Step 1: we create a single row of seven cells all set to one, representing the top row where every department is reachable by exactly one route. Step 2: for the second stage we walk columns one to six, adding the cell to the left into each cell, so the row becomes one, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Step 3: for the third stage we again add the left cell into each, so the row becomes one, three, six, ten, fifteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight. Step 4: each cell now holds the number of routes from the start to that stage-and-department corner. Step 5: the last cell holds twenty-eight, so there are twenty-eight distinct approval routes from intake to final sign-off.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths counts the routes across a grid when only rightward and downward moves are allowed, and the recurrence falls straight out of the movement rule. Any cell can only be entered from the cell directly above it or the cell directly to its left, and those two sets of paths never overlap, so the number of ways to reach a cell is simply the sum of the ways to reach those two neighbours. The entire top row and the entire left column each have exactly one path, which gives the base cases.

Because each cell depends only on the row above and the cell immediately to the left, I collapse the grid to a single row initialised to all ones and update it left to right. In that single row, the value already sitting in a cell represents the cell above, and the value just to its left represents the cell to the left, so a single addition does the work. This runs in time proportional to the product of the dimensions and space proportional to the smaller dimension. I also mention the closed-form binomial answer, which chooses the down moves among the total moves in constant time but can overflow for large grids.

At the National Bank of India I used this to model a loan approval workflow as a grid, where a request moved either to the next approval stage or across to the next department, and risk analysts wanted the number of distinct approval routes from intake to final sign-off. I computed it with the single-row dynamic programming. Explaining the above-plus-left recurrence, the base-case row and column, and the single-row space optimisation is what shows an interviewer I can derive a counting recurrence directly from a problem's movement constraints.
